title: 2026-09-25 Helix DataGuard private deploy control-plane security sync
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Helix DataGuard team through options for a private control plane deployment: control plane placement (Redwood-managed vs customer-managed), network isolation patterns, egress gateway strategy, and KMS integration models. Key concerns were auditability for SOC 2, SSO provisioning, and how to enforce tight egress controls while preserving low-latency inference. Action items include an architecture sketch, benchmark notes for canary, and delivery of SOC 2 artifacts and KMS integration guide.
next_steps: Redwood to send private-deploy architecture sketch and RTP (routing) options
Priya to schedule a 1-hour tech lab to validate egress gateway throughput next week
Helix to provide a list of required compliance artifacts and key rotation windows
Set pilot start date (target: second week of October)
action_items: Priya Kapoor: prepare architecture sketch + egress options (due 2026-09-29)
Marcus Chen: share network ACLs and current VPC layout (due 2026-09-30)
Jordan Lee: provide SOC 2 summary and client-facing security deck (due 2026-09-27)
Diego Morales: validate OKTA SAML metadata and SSO test user (due 2026-09-28)
Lina Vu: list of required audit log retention windows and offsite storage regs (due 2026-10-02)
meeting_header:
Date: 2026-09-25 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Location: Zoom | Recording: Enabled
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Miguel Santos (Redwood Solutions); Marcus Chen (Helix Head of Infra), Aisha Rahman (Helix CISO), Diego Morales (Platform Eng), Lina Vu (Compliance), Samir Patel (Network Eng)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna run through the private control plane options, network isolation and especially the egress play— egress patterns that you asked about. Marcus, do you wanna kick off with your main constraints?
[00:18] Marcus Chen: Yeah thanks, Jordan. main thing for us is we need end-to-end auditability for SOC two so logs, retention and chain of custody basically. second, we have strict egress rules — only allowed outbound to a handful of endpoints. latency matters because the product is real-time scoring.
[00:33] Aisha Rahman: And just to add, from a compliance POV we need proof of key management, ideally BYOK and HSM-backed, plus a key rotation window documented. we can't have vendor-held keys without a KMS contract.
[00:45] Priya Kapoor: Understood. quick overview: Redwood supports three private control plane modes — fully customer-managed control plane in your VPC, a hybrid where control plane is in a private subnetwork we manage but peered, and a Redwood-managed private tenancy with strict egress gateways. Each has tradeoffs for ops surface and auditability.
[01:04] Diego Morales: Can you expand on the hybrid? what lives in our VPC vs Redwood?
[01:09] Priya Kapoor: Sure — in hybrid the control-plane components that store secrets and audit logs live in your VPC (you run the stateful services or we deploy them as containers into your cluster), while the stateless metrics and telemetry can flow to Redwood-managed endpoints through a locked-down peering with enforced ACLs. The key is to give you ownership of KMS material and the audit log storage.
[01:30] Samir Patel: That peering sounds ok, but how do we prevent accidental egress? we run strict firewall — everything blocked except approved egress. will the control plane need new firewall rules?
[01:38] Priya Kapoor: Yes, minimal firewall openings for control-plane health checks and the egress gateway IP ranges. We recommend an egress gateway pattern: all outbound inference traffic and logging is tunneled through a dedicated NAT/Egress appliance you control. Redwood can provide a small set of stable destination IPs and an allowlist rather than broad ranges.
[01:55] Jordan Lee: To add, we also support a TLS-mTLS option for control-plane and data-plane comms so connections can be terminated at your egress gateway for inspection, and the control plane will validate client certs.
[02:08] Aisha Rahman: When you say logs stored in our S3, are those immutable? we need append-only retention and tamper evidence for SOC two.
[02:17] Miguel Santos: Good call — we can ship logs to your S3 with SSE-KMS and object lock enabled; we also support pushing a digest to a third-party ledger for tamper evidence. The KMS can be BYOK — we support AWS KMS and HSM-backed keys via import.
[02:33] Speaker 1: umm, small note, some customers ask about rotation windows — how frequently can keys rotate without breaking cached KV?
[02:40] Priya Kapoor: We recommend a 90-day rotation for root keys and 30–60 day for data keys. For KV cache, Redwood includes a key-rotation handshake; sessions carry a short lived token re-encrypted with the new key, so cache misses are minimal. But we'll detail that in the doc.
[02:58] Marcus Chen: Ok, latency — you mentioned egress gateway, won't that add 40–100ms tail?
[03:05] Jordan Lee: Depends on topology. If the egress gateway is in the same AZ and you use the accelerated private-path routing, typically 5–25ms added. If it's across a different region or goes via inspection tooling, you could see more. That's why we propose a canary bench.
[03:22] Diego Morales: About RBAC and provisioning — we use Okta and SCIM. how does Redwood handle tenant separation in private deploys?
[03:30] Priya Kapoor: We have two models. Single-tenant VPC isolations where each customer has dedicated runtime nodes — RBAC enforced via your identity provider and our platform proxies checks against SAML/SCIM groups. Or multi-tenant but logically isolated where tokens and mTLS certificates enforce tenancy boundaries. For strict compliance, single-tenant VPC is the recommended path.
[03:48] Aisha Rahman: Do you have SOC two artifacts showing control mappings for those models? we need evidence for auditors.
[03:55] Jordan Lee: Yes, I'll share a SOC two summary and the control mapping spreadsheet. we also have ISO 27001 scope docs that map to the deployment modes.
[04:06] Lina Vu: What's your proposed audit log retention default and can we set different retention per log class?
[04:13] Priya Kapoor: Default is 13 months online; we support tiered retention: 13 months online, long-term cold archive to our S3 or your storage for compliance windows up to seven years. And yes, retention can be set per log type — access logs, admin audit, inference request traces.
[04:31] Marcus Chen: Ok, egress: if a model tries to autodownload artifacts, can we block that at the NAT?
[04:37] Miguel Santos: Absolutely, egress gateway with a proxy can do URL allowlisting and block package registries. We can also provide a hardened image that contains allowed model bundles; the model onboarding process then goes through your approval.
[04:50] Diego Morales: For private models and quantized artifacts, are they encrypted at rest?
[04:54] Priya Kapoor: Yes — at-rest encryption with your KMS key (BYOK) and optional FIPS 140-2 HSM wrapping for keys.
[05:02] Samir Patel: On firewalling, we're big on microsegmentation. can Redwood's runtime speak to our service mesh?
[05:09] Priya Kapoor: We have integrations for Istio/Linkerd to surface fine-grained mTLS within the cluster. For host-level segmentation, we recommend security groups + pod-level policies. We can instrument sidecars that emit the minimal telemetry you need for audits.
[05:26] Jordan Lee: Quick check — any blockers on identity and provisioning?
[05:29] Diego Morales: We need SCIM for automated group sync and a test SSO setup.
[05:33] Jordan Lee: We'll get you metadata and a test SAML file.
[05:36] Aisha Rahman: What about anomaly detection on logs — can Redwood push to our SIEM?
[05:41] Miguel Santos: Yes, we can stream logs over secure forwarders to your SIEM (SPLUNK, Sumo, Datadog). We can also ship JSON with field-level masking for PII.
[05:53] Speaker 2: There's sometimes imperfect transcribing here, sorry — but can you explain ingress rules?
[05:58] Priya Kapoor: Ingress is strictly inbound only from your control network; we offer a bastion/controller API endpoint with static IPs. For models invoked from public internet, we recommend a private API gateway in front of the runtime with request validation and WAF.
[06:15] Marcus Chen: Will the runtime probe external TTL DNS? we prefer no external name resolution from private subnets.
[06:21] Priya Kapoor: We can disable outbound DNS and use VPC resolver endpoints. All external resolution goes through your resolver.
[06:28] Jordan Lee: Let's talk about fallback — if a private node fails, do you failover to hosted?
[06:33] Diego Morales: that's a policy question for us — prefer no data leaving region.
[06:36] Priya Kapoor: We support policy-based routing: you can set failover to Redwood-hosted but only for non-sensitive workloads; for regulated workloads we do in-region private failover to a standby cluster. That behavior is configurable per environment.
[06:50] Samir Patel: Regarding HSM: is there latency hit for every crypto op to HSM?
[06:54] Miguel Santos: Typically HSM ops are used for root key unwraps; bulk data encryption uses data keys cached in memory. So HSM calls are infrequent — during rotation or key unwrap. We'll show the flow.
[07:07] Aisha Rahman: For SOC 2, we need proof of separation of duties. how does Redwood separate ops from infra?
[07:13] Jordan Lee: Our ops run in a dedicated org account with RBAC, audit trails and approved runbooks. We'll provide an operations org diagram and control descriptions.
[07:25] Diego Morales: Can you walk through an example of an audit trail for a model inference request?
[07:29] Priya Kapoor: Sure: inference request hits your private API gateway -> routed to runtime -> runtime emits a trace with request id, model version, token usage and user id (if PII redaction applied) -> trace shipped to your S3 or SIEM with immutable keys. We keep request-level hashes for tamper-proofing.
[07:47] Speaker 3: the transcripts here sometimes miss words but, small question — can we store request traces in our on-prem object store?
[07:53] Miguel Santos: Yes, we can ship to S3-compatible endpoints including on-prem solutions. We just need connectivity (egress to your object store endpoints) and credentials stored in your KMS.
[08:05] Marcus Chen: Any prebuilt policy templates for firewall rules and NAC?
[08:09] Priya Kapoor: We have a repo of terraform modules and example security groups, NAC templates and egress gateway config. We'll share a starter kit.
[08:18] Jordan Lee: Let's cover a timeline for a pilot — tech lab to validate egress and KMS then small canary with 1 node and 100 qps. Any objections?
[08:27] Diego Morales: Sounds good. need to confirm bandwidth.
[08:30] Priya Kapoor: For the lab we'll provide a test harness and synthetic workload, and we'll capture 95/99p latency.
[08:36] Aisha Rahman: For compliance, we need a hit list of controls you map to SOC two.
[08:40] Jordan Lee: I'll attach the control mapping.
[08:42] Samir Patel: what about network IDS/IPS? can we inline it?
[08:46] Miguel Santos: Yes inline IDS is supported at the egress gateway. We can also mirror traffic to your monitoring stack for analysis.
[08:55] Diego Morales: For SCIM, does Redwood push group changes or just read?
[08:59] Priya Kapoor: We support both push and pull flows; push SCIM provisioning is available for automation.
[09:05] Marcus Chen: Anything that would break our existing pod policies?
[09:08] Priya Kapoor: Our runtime respects existing pod security policies; we can help with compatibility patches.
[09:13] Jordan Lee: I'm going to summarize next steps at the end. Any other blockers?
[09:17] Lina Vu: GDPR note — we need to ensure data residency for EU customers inside EU regions. Does Redwood support EU-only storage for audit logs?
[09:25] Miguel Santos: Yes, regionalized log storage and regional control planes in EU and APAC are available. We'll annotate the architecture doc with region boundaries.
[09:35] Marcus Chen: one more — can we get a fail-open or fail-closed option on the egress gateway?
[09:40] Priya Kapoor: Both supported but default is fail-closed for security. Fail-open for non-critical dev lanes is possible with a different policy.
[09:49] Jordan Lee: Great. we'll follow up with documentation.
[09:52] Diego Morales: thanks everyone.
[52:00] End of meeting (recording stopped).
